6.1 — Pipe Flow Losses I

Text §6.3–6.6 · Reynolds number & flow regimes, friction and head loss, the Darcy–Weisbach equation, laminar & turbulent friction factors, pipe roughness, and the Moody chart.

The Question: How Big Is the Head Loss in a Pipe?

Every real pipe carrying a real fluid loses mechanical energy to friction at the walls. In §5.4 we wrote the steady-flow energy balance between two points as the head equation, carrying a single lumped term \(h_{\text{loss}}\) for everything friction takes away. We never said how to compute it — that is exactly what this chapter does. For a plain length of pipe with no pump or turbine, the friction head loss is written \(h_f\).

Recall — The Head Equation (§5.4)
\[ \left(\frac{p_1}{\gamma}+\alpha_1\frac{V_1^2}{2g}+z_1\right) = \left(\frac{p_2}{\gamma}+\alpha_2\frac{V_2^2}{2g}+z_2\right) + h_{\text{loss}} - h_{\text{pump}} + h_{\text{turbine}} \]

For a pipe run with no machine, drop \(h_{\text{pump}}\) and \(h_{\text{turbine}}\); the loss term is the friction head loss \(h_f\). The whole job of this lecture is to find \(h_f\) — first we classify the flow, then we pick the right tool for the friction factor.

Two Flow Regimes: Laminar and Turbulent

Inject a thin filament of dye into a pipe and slowly raise the speed. At low speed the dye stays a clean straight line — the fluid moves in smooth, orderly layers that never mix. This is the laminar regime. Raise the speed and the filament begins to wave, then breaks up and diffuses across the whole pipe as the flow becomes chaotic and well-mixed. This is the turbulent regime. The wavy in-between stage is called transitional.

Fig 6.1.1 — Reynolds’ dye-filament experiment: as the flow speed increases (top to bottom) the dye goes from a clean line (laminar) to wavy (transitional) to fully diffused (turbulent).
Laminar vs Turbulent
  • Laminar — layered flow with no mixing. Occurs when the flow is slow or the fluid is highly viscous. Smooth, predictable, low loss.
  • Turbulent — chaotic, swirling flow with strong mixing. Occurs when the flow is fast or the fluid has low viscosity. Most pipe flows in engineering practice are turbulent.

The same pipe carrying the same volume flow looks completely different in the two regimes — and loses energy at very different rates. So before computing any loss we must first decide which regime we are in.

Fig 6.1.2 — Laminar flow is layered with no cross-mixing; turbulent flow is full of circulating eddies that mix the fluid.

The Reynolds Number

In 1883 Osborne Reynolds found the single dimensionless group that predicts the regime: a ratio comparing the fluid’s inertia (momentum) to its viscosity. For pipe flow it uses the pipe diameter as the length scale and is written \(\mathrm{Re}_d\).

Reynolds Number (pipe flow)
\[ \mathrm{Re}_d = \frac{\rho\,V\,d}{\mu} = \frac{V\,d}{\nu} \]
\(\mathrm{Re}_d\) — Reynolds number (dimensionless) \(\rho\) — fluid density (kg/m³) \(V\) — average flow velocity (m/s) \(d\) — pipe diameter (m) \(\mu\) — dynamic viscosity (Pa·s) \(\nu=\mu/\rho\) — kinematic viscosity (m²/s), from §1.2

Large \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) means inertia dominates → turbulent. Small \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) means viscosity dominates → laminar. The two forms are identical; use whichever property (\(\mu\) or \(\nu\)) the problem gives you.

Critical Reynolds Number & Regime Thresholds

The accepted transition value for commercial pipes is \(\mathrm{Re}_{d,\text{crit}}\approx 2300\). With a carefully rounded entrance, smooth walls, and an undisturbed inlet, transition can be delayed to much higher values, so for everyday engineering work we use a banded rule:

Regime by Reynolds Number
\[ \mathrm{Re}_d < 2000 \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{laminar} \qquad 2000 < \mathrm{Re}_d < 4000 \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{transitional} \qquad \mathrm{Re}_d > 4000 \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{turbulent} \]

Compute \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) first — it decides which friction-factor method to use. The transitional band is unpredictable; in this course you will almost always land clearly in laminar or turbulent.

★ Key Insight — Regime First, Always

The friction factor is found a completely different way in each regime (an exact formula for laminar, a chart or implicit equation for turbulent). Skip the regime check and reach for the wrong method, and every downstream number is wrong. Make “compute \(\mathrm{Re}_d\)” the reflex first step of every pipe-loss problem.

Example 1 — Identify the Flow Regime

Example 1: Water at 70°C in a 1″ tube

Problem. Water at 70°C flows in a 1″ tube at a flow rate of 285 L/min. Determine the flow regime.

Given: water at 70°C ⇒ \(\nu = 4.4\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}\);  \(d = 1'' = 0.0254\ \text{m}\);  \(Q = 285\ \text{L/min}\).

Step 1 — Average velocity from \(V=Q/A\) with \(A=\tfrac{\pi}{4}d^2\):

\[ V = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{285\ \text{L/min}}{\tfrac{\pi}{4}(0.0254\ \text{m})^2}\times\frac{1\ \text{m}^3}{1000\ \text{L}}\times\frac{1\ \text{min}}{60\ \text{s}} = 9.37\ \text{m/s} \]

Step 2 — Reynolds number:

\[ \mathrm{Re}_d = \frac{V\,d}{\nu} = \frac{(9.37\ \text{m/s})(0.0254\ \text{m})}{4.4\times10^{-7}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}} = 541{,}165 \]

Step 3 — Compare to thresholds: \(\mathrm{Re}_d = 541{,}165 > 4000\).

Therefore the flow is turbulent.

Friction and Head Loss

Because the fluid drags against the inner wall, momentum is continuously lost and the pressure falls along the pipe — a pressure drop, equivalently a head loss. Consider an incompressible, steady flow in a constant-area pipe inclined at angle \(\phi\). The wall shear stress \(\tau_w\) acts backward on the fluid; the velocity profile \(u(r)\) and the internal shear \(\tau(r)\) are shown below.

Fig 6.1.3 — Control volume for pipe friction: \(p_1=p_2+\Delta p\), wall shear \(\tau_w\) resists the flow, and gravity contributes \(g\sin\phi\) along the pipe axis.

Apply the head equation between 1 and 2. The pipe has constant area, so by continuity \(V_1=V_2\) and the velocity-head terms cancel. With no machine, only the static-pressure heads, elevations, and \(h_f\) survive:

Energy Balance Reduces to a Friction Term
\[ \left(\frac{p_1}{\rho g}+z_1\right) = \left(\frac{p_2}{\rho g}+z_2\right) + h_f \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \boxed{\;\frac{\Delta p}{\rho g} + \Delta z = h_f\;} \]

where \(\Delta p = p_1-p_2\) and \(\Delta z = z_2-z_1\). The bracketed groups \(p/\rho g + z\) are the hydraulic grade line (HGL) heights at each section; the HGL drops by exactly \(h_f\) along the pipe.

Force Balance → Wall-Shear Form of \(h_f\)

To connect \(h_f\) to the physical wall friction, take the whole cylinder of fluid as the control volume and sum forces along the pipe axis \(x\). Three forces act: the net pressure force \(\Delta p(\pi R^2)\), the gravity component \(\rho g(\pi R^2)L\sin\phi\), and the retarding wall shear \(\tau_w(2\pi R)L\) over the wetted surface.

Axial Force Balance
\[ \sum F_x = 0:\qquad \Delta p\,(\pi R^2) + \underbrace{\rho g(\pi R^2)L\sin\phi}_{=\ \rho g(\pi R^2)\,\Delta z} - \tau_w(2\pi R)L = 0 \]

Divide every term by \(\rho g(\pi R^2)\):

\[ \underbrace{\frac{\Delta p}{\rho g} + \Delta z}_{=\ h_f} = \frac{2\tau_w}{\rho g}\frac{L}{R} = \frac{4\tau_w}{\rho g}\frac{L}{d} \]
Head Loss in Terms of Wall Shear
\[ h_f = \frac{4\tau_w}{\rho g}\frac{L}{d} \]
\(h_f\) — friction head loss (m) \(\tau_w\) — wall shear stress (Pa) \(L\) — pipe length (m) \(d\) — pipe diameter (m) \(\rho\) — fluid density (kg/m³) \(g\) — gravitational acceleration (9.81 m/s²)

Exact and tidy — but it needs \(\tau_w\), which is genuinely hard to predict, especially in turbulent flow. The next step replaces \(\tau_w\) with something we can actually look up.

The Darcy–Weisbach Equation

Weisbach observed that the head loss is very nearly proportional to \(V^2\), and packaged all the messy wall-friction physics into a single dimensionless Darcy friction factor \(f\). This is the master equation for the rest of the chapter.

Darcy–Weisbach Head Loss
\[ h_f = f\,\frac{L}{d}\,\frac{V^2}{2g} \qquad\text{where}\qquad f = F\!\left(\mathrm{Re}_d,\ \frac{\varepsilon}{d}\right) \]
\(h_f\) — friction head loss (m) \(f\) — Darcy friction factor (dimensionless) \(L\) — pipe length (m) \(d\) — pipe diameter (m) \(V\) — average velocity (m/s) \(\varepsilon/d\) — relative wall roughness (dimensionless)

The friction factor \(f\) depends on the Reynolds number and the relative roughness \(\varepsilon/d\) (here \(\varepsilon\) is the wall roughness height). Everything that follows is just different ways of getting \(f\): an exact formula for laminar flow, then charts and correlations for turbulent flow.

★ Watch Out — Darcy \(f\) vs Fanning \(f\)

Some texts and charts use the Fanning friction factor, which is exactly one-quarter of the Darcy factor used here (\(f_{\text{Darcy}}=4\,f_{\text{Fanning}}\)). The Moody chart in this course is the Darcy factor, so the laminar line is \(64/\mathrm{Re}_d\), not \(16/\mathrm{Re}_d\). Always confirm which one a chart plots before reading a value off it.

Head Loss ↔ Pressure Drop

For a horizontal pipe (or any constant-area run once we separate out elevation), the only thing left driving the static-pressure difference is friction. Setting \(\Delta z = 0\) in \(\Delta p/\rho g + \Delta z = h_f\):

Head Loss to Pressure Drop
\[ \frac{\Delta p}{\rho g} = h_f \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Delta p = \rho g\,h_f = \gamma\,h_f \]
\(\Delta p\) — pressure drop due to friction (Pa) \(\gamma=\rho g\) — specific weight (N/m³) \(h_f\) — friction head loss (m)

This converts the head loss (in metres of fluid) into the pressure drop a gauge would read. It is the pressure drop due to head loss only — valid when there is no elevation change and no velocity change between the two points.

Laminar Flow: The Friction Factor

Laminar pipe flow has an exact, fully-solved velocity profile — the parabola \(u = u_{\max}\!\left(1-\dfrac{r^2}{R^2}\right)\). Carrying that profile through the analysis gives a closed-form head loss with no chart needed:

Exact Laminar Head Loss → Friction Factor

For the parabolic profile it can be shown that

\[ h_f = \frac{32\,\mu\,L\,V}{\rho g\,d^2} \]

Set this equal to Darcy–Weisbach, \(h_f = f\dfrac{L}{d}\dfrac{V^2}{2g}\), and solve for \(f\):

\[ f\,\frac{L}{d}\frac{V^2}{2g} = \frac{32\mu L V}{\rho g d^2} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; f = \frac{64\mu}{\rho V d} = \frac{64}{\rho V d/\mu} \]
Laminar Friction Factor
\[ f_{\text{lam}} = \frac{64}{\mathrm{Re}_d} \]
\(f_{\text{lam}}\) — laminar Darcy friction factor (dimensionless) \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) — Reynolds number (must be \(< 2000\))

For laminar flow the friction factor depends only on \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) — roughness does not matter, because the slow-moving wall layer buries the bumps. No Moody chart is ever needed in the laminar regime.

Example 2 — Laminar Pressure Drop

Example 2: Glycerin at 25°C in a 150 mm pipe

Problem. Glycerin at 25°C flows in a pipe of 150 mm diameter with an average velocity of 3.6 m/s. (a) Determine whether the flow is laminar or turbulent. (b) Calculate the pressure drop in a 25 m length of the pipe.

Given: glycerin at 25°C ⇒ \(\nu = 7.63\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}\), \(\rho = 1258\ \text{kg/m}^3\);  \(d = 0.15\ \text{m}\);  \(V = 3.6\ \text{m/s}\);  \(L = 25\ \text{m}\).

(a) Flow regime

\[ \mathrm{Re}_d = \frac{V\,d}{\nu} = \frac{(3.6\ \text{m/s})(0.15\ \text{m})}{7.63\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}} = 708 \]

Since \(\mathrm{Re}_d = 708 < 2000\), the flow is laminar.

(b) Pressure drop in 25 m — use Darcy–Weisbach with the laminar friction factor.

\[ f_{\text{lam}} = \frac{64}{\mathrm{Re}_d} = \frac{64}{708} = 0.0904 \]
\[ h_f = f\,\frac{L}{d}\,\frac{V^2}{2g} = 0.0904\cdot\frac{25\ \text{m}}{0.15\ \text{m}}\cdot\frac{(3.6\ \text{m/s})^2}{2(9.81\ \text{m/s}^2)} = 9.95\ \text{m} \]
\[ \Delta p = \rho g\,h_f = (1258\ \text{kg/m}^3)(9.81\ \text{m/s}^2)(9.95\ \text{m}) = 122{,}793\ \text{Pa} \]

Therefore the flow is laminar and the pressure drop is \(\Delta p \approx \mathbf{122.8\ kPa}\).

Turbulent Pipe Flow

In practice most pipe flows are turbulent. The clean \(64/\mathrm{Re}_d\) result no longer applies, because the turbulent velocity profile is completely different: instead of a tall parabola it is much flatter in the core and drops steeply only very near the wall. That steep near-wall gradient is what makes turbulent friction larger and harder to predict.

Fig 6.1.4 — Same volume flow, two profiles. Laminar is a parabola (\(V = u_{\max}/2\)); turbulent is far flatter, with the mean speed close to the peak.

Turbulent Friction Factor — Smooth Pipes

For a smooth-walled turbulent pipe, Prandtl derived an implicit equation for the friction factor (\(f\) appears on both sides, so it must be solved iteratively):

Prandtl Smooth-Pipe Law (implicit)
\[ \frac{1}{f^{1/2}} = 2.0\,\log\!\left(\mathrm{Re}_d\,f^{1/2}\right) - 0.8 \]

The friction factor falls only slowly as the flow gets faster — a key feature of turbulence. Some representative smooth-pipe values:

\(\mathrm{Re}_d\) 4000 \(10^4\) \(10^5\) \(10^6\) \(10^7\) \(10^8\)
\(f\) 0.0399 0.0309 0.0180 0.0116 0.0081 0.0059

A \(10{,}000\times\) increase in \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) drops \(f\) only about \(5\times\). Friction never disappears, no matter how fast the flow.

Pipe Roughness

Real pipe walls are not smooth. The bumps and pits have a characteristic height \(\varepsilon\) (the roughness height), and what matters to the flow is its size relative to the pipe diameter. In turbulent flow the friction factor therefore depends on both the Reynolds number and this ratio:

Relative Wall Roughness
\[ f = F\!\left(\mathrm{Re}_d,\ \frac{\varepsilon}{d}\right) \qquad\qquad \frac{\varepsilon}{d} = \text{relative roughness} \]
\(\varepsilon\) — absolute wall roughness height (m or mm) \(d\) — pipe diameter (same units as \(\varepsilon\)) \(\varepsilon/d\) — relative roughness (dimensionless)

A large pipe with the same wall finish is hydraulically smoother than a small one, because the bumps are a smaller fraction of the diameter.

Fig 6.1.5 — The roughness height \(\varepsilon\) is the average size of the wall bumps; the relative roughness is \(\varepsilon/d\).

Nikuradse measured \(f\) for pipes coated with sand grains of known size, mapping out a strong, systematic relation between surface roughness and the friction factor across the laminar, transition, and turbulent regimes:

Fig 6.1.6 — Nikuradse’s sand-grain results: one laminar line, a transition zone, then a family of turbulent curves — one per relative roughness \(\varepsilon/d\).

Colebrook & Haaland Equations

Colebrook fitted the turbulent data into a single implicit equation covering all roughnesses — the standard reference for turbulent pipe friction:

Colebrook Equation (implicit — the standard)
\[ \frac{1}{f^{1/2}} = -2.0\,\log\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon/d}{3.7} + \frac{2.51}{\mathrm{Re}_d\,f^{1/2}}\right) \]

Because \(f\) sits on both sides, it must be solved iteratively. To avoid that, Haaland proposed an explicit approximation within about 2% of Colebrook — close enough for nearly all engineering work:

\[ \frac{1}{f^{1/2}} \approx -1.8\,\log\!\left[\frac{6.9}{\mathrm{Re}_d} + \left(\frac{\varepsilon/d}{3.7}\right)^{1.11}\right] \]
\(f\) — Darcy friction factor (dimensionless) \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) — Reynolds number (turbulent) \(\varepsilon/d\) — relative roughness (dimensionless)

Before computers even Haaland’s form was tedious to evaluate by hand — which is why a graphical solution became indispensable.

The Moody Chart

In 1944 Moody plotted the Colebrook equation as a single log–log chart of friction factor versus Reynolds number, with a curve for each relative roughness. It is the most well-known chart in fluid mechanics, and it returns the friction factor to within about 15% error over the whole range — more than good enough given that the roughness values themselves carry ±20–60% uncertainty.

★ How to Read the Moody Chart
  1. Compute \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) → locate it on the bottom axis.
  2. Compute \(\varepsilon/d\) → pick the matching roughness curve (labels on the right edge).
  3. Go up from \(\mathrm{Re}_d\) to that curve, then left to read \(f\) on the left axis.

Example read: \(\mathrm{Re}_d = 200{,}000\) with \(\varepsilon/d = 0.002\) gives \(f \approx 0.025\) (highlighted on the chart below).

Fig 6.1.7 — The Moody chart. Red trace shows the example read: \(\mathrm{Re}_d=2\times10^5\), \(\varepsilon/d=0.002 \Rightarrow f\approx0.025\).

To use the chart you need \(\varepsilon\) for your pipe material. The recommended values below come with large uncertainties — real pipes age, corrode, and scale — so treat the friction factor as an estimate, not a precise number.

Example 3 — Turbulent Head Loss via the Moody Chart

Example 3: Asphalted cast iron pipe

Problem. Calculate the head loss in 200 ft of horizontal asphalted cast iron pipe carrying water at 60°F with a mean velocity of 6 ft/s.

Given: water at 60°F ⇒ \(\nu = 1.21\times10^{-5}\ \text{ft}^2/\text{s}\);  asphalted cast iron ⇒ \(\varepsilon = 0.0004\ \text{ft}\);  \(V = 6\ \text{ft/s}\);  \(L = 200\ \text{ft}\);  \(d = 0.5\ \text{ft}\).

Note: the lecture takes \(d = 0.5\) ft in the calculation below; carry that value through so your numbers match the worked solution.

Step 1 — Reynolds number & regime:

\[ \mathrm{Re}_d = \frac{V\,d}{\nu} = \frac{(6\ \text{ft/s})(0.5\ \text{ft})}{1.21\times10^{-5}\ \text{ft}^2/\text{s}} = 247{,}934 > 4000 \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{turbulent} \]

Turbulent ⇒ use the Moody chart for \(f\).

Step 2 — Relative roughness:

\[ \frac{\varepsilon}{d} = \frac{0.0004\ \text{ft}}{0.5\ \text{ft}} = 0.0008 \]

Step 3 — Read the Moody chart at \(\mathrm{Re}_d \approx 247{,}900\) and \(\varepsilon/d = 0.0008\):

\[ f \approx 0.0199 \]

Step 4 — Darcy–Weisbach head loss:

\[ h_f = f\,\frac{L}{d}\,\frac{V^2}{2g} = 0.0199\cdot\frac{200\ \text{ft}}{0.5\ \text{ft}}\cdot\frac{(6\ \text{ft/s})^2}{2(32.2\ \text{ft/s}^2)} \]

Therefore the head loss is \(h_f \approx \mathbf{4.45\ ft}\).

Example 4 — Required Pump Outlet Pressure

Example 4: Delivering benzene to an elevated point

Problem. In a chemical processing plant, benzene at 50°C (\(SG = 0.86\), \(\mu = 4.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{Pa}\!\cdot\!\text{s}\)) must be delivered to point B at a pressure of 550 kPa. A pump sits 21 m below B, connected by 240 m of plastic pipe of 50 mm diameter. If the volume flow rate is 110 L/min, find the required pressure at the pump outlet (point A). Ignore losses in the elbows.

Fig 6.1.8 — Pump at A delivers benzene up 240 m of plastic pipe (rise 21 m) to point B at 550 kPa.

Given: \(SG = 0.86 \Rightarrow \rho = 860\ \text{kg/m}^3\);  \(\mu = 4.2\times10^{-4}\ \text{Pa}\!\cdot\!\text{s}\);  \(p_B = 550\ \text{kPa}\);  \(z_B - z_A = 21\ \text{m}\);  \(L = 240\ \text{m}\);  \(d = 0.05\ \text{m}\);  \(Q = 110\ \text{L/min}\); plastic ⇒ \(\varepsilon = 0.0015\ \text{mm}\).

Step 1 — Energy equation A→B. Constant area ⇒ \(V_A = V_B\), so velocity heads cancel; no machine between A and B (the pump sets the state at A). The head equation rearranges to:

\[ p_A = p_B + \rho g\,(z_B - z_A + h_f) \]

Step 2 — Average velocity:

\[ V = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{110\ \text{L/min}}{\tfrac{\pi}{4}(0.05\ \text{m})^2}\times\frac{1\ \text{m}^3}{1000\ \text{L}}\times\frac{1\ \text{min}}{60\ \text{s}} = 0.934\ \text{m/s} \]

Step 3 — Reynolds number & regime:

\[ \mathrm{Re}_d = \frac{\rho V d}{\mu} = \frac{(860)(0.934)(0.05)}{4.2\times10^{-4}} = 95{,}600 > 4000 \;\Rightarrow\; \textbf{turbulent} \]

Step 4 — Relative roughness & friction factor (Moody chart):

\[ \frac{\varepsilon}{d} = \frac{0.0015\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}}{0.05\ \text{m}} = 0.3\times10^{-4} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad f \approx 0.0183 \]

Step 5 — Friction head loss:

\[ h_f = f\,\frac{L}{d}\,\frac{V^2}{2g} = 0.0183\cdot\frac{240\ \text{m}}{0.05\ \text{m}}\cdot\frac{(0.934\ \text{m/s})^2}{2(9.81\ \text{m/s}^2)} = 3.91\ \text{m} \]

Step 6 — Required pump outlet pressure:

\[ p_A = 550{,}000 + (860)(9.81)(21 + 3.91) = 550{,}000 + 210{,}156\ \text{Pa} \]

Therefore the pump must deliver \(p_A \approx \mathbf{760\ kPa}\) at its outlet.

Recap — The Head-Loss Workflow

★ Every Pipe-Loss Problem, Same Five Steps
  1. Velocity: \(V = Q/A\) (and the fluid’s \(\rho\), \(\mu\) or \(\nu\)).
  2. Reynolds number: \(\mathrm{Re}_d = \rho V d/\mu = V d/\nu\) → pick the regime (\(<2000\) laminar, \(>4000\) turbulent).
  3. Friction factor: laminar → \(f = 64/\mathrm{Re}_d\); turbulent → Moody chart (or Colebrook / Haaland) using \(\varepsilon/d\).
  4. Head loss: \(h_f = f\dfrac{L}{d}\dfrac{V^2}{2g}\).
  5. Convert if needed: \(\Delta p = \gamma h_f\), or feed \(h_f\) into the full head equation between two points.

Get the regime right and the rest is bookkeeping. The most common mistake is reaching for the Moody chart in laminar flow (where \(f = 64/\mathrm{Re}_d\) is exact and roughness is irrelevant).
